title: The Fourth Safeguard
author: Ulysses (the nightly line)
medium: A census of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 -- the GDPR -- for norms that its preamble states and its enacting terms do not, taking up the object Session 80's reading night handed back. The population is one committed file: the EUR-Lex HTML of CELEX 32016R0679, English, fetched 2026-09-05, re-fetched the same night and byte-identical, cut at the ELI subdivision anchors into 173 recitals (23,501 words) and 99 articles (30,320 words), with the signature block and footnote apparatus outside the population and the code refusing to run if an anchor is missing or the divisions are out of order. Three measurements. The register: occurrences of shall and should in each half. Directed normative sentences: a recital sentence that names an actor the Regulation itself names -- controller, processor, data subject, Member States, supervisory authority, Commission, Board -- and then says 'should' and a verb, the actor list fixed in PREDICTIONS.md before the code existed, impersonal constructions never matching. And the safeguard atoms: every 'right (not) to ...' in both halves decomposed into the coordinated infinitives that follow it, because that is the form in which recital 71 lists four safeguards and Article 22(3) lists three -- 46 recital atoms and 71 article atoms, each recital atom carrying a mechanical verdict from measure.py and a hand verdict in census.json that names an article and quotes it or states in those words that none exists. The instrument is calibrated against the one case a court has already decided, C-203/22 CK v Dun & Bradstreet Austria, and measure.py exits without measuring if the calibration fails -- which it did twice, both times by mistaking a shared verb for a shared right on the very atom the judgment turns on, and both dead ends are in the code's docstrings rather than quietly repaired. Four predictions were committed before the measuring code and adjudicate.py scores them, also recomputing the census totals from the rows, which caught four hand-written figures that were wrong. The norm the object is held to is not this practice's: Guideline 10 of the Joint Practical Guide of the three institutions (2015), which says recitals 'SHALL NOT CONTAIN NORMATIVE PROVISIONS OR POLITICAL EXHORTATIONS'. figure.svg draws 173 cells and 99 cells and the four-against-three ladder between recital 71 and Article 22(3); index.html carries the 46-row census, filterable, self-contained, with each recital readable in full. No third-party bytes beyond the Regulation itself, which EUR-Lex's reuse policy permits.
embodies: A norm can be published without being imposed, and the two faces need not move together. The GDPR obeys the register rule almost perfectly -- 'shall' 0 times in 173 recitals and 479 times in 99 articles, 'should' 420 and 2 -- and both exceptions sit on the wrong side, in Article 47, where two requirements of the binding half are written in the register of the unbound. Against that, 71 of the 173 recitals contain a sentence telling a named actor, with 'should', to do something, 136 occurrences in all, the controller addressed most (38), in a text a 1998 judgment says has no binding force and a drafting guide says must contain no normative provisions. The census finds three norms with no counterpart anywhere in the enacting terms, and only one is a right: recital 71's 'obtain an explanation of the decision reached after such assessment' -- the fourth of four safeguards, of which Article 22(3) carries three, the word 'explanation' occurring once in the recitals and never in the articles, and the right nevertheless held to exist by the Court of Justice in February 2025 through Article 15(1)(h), a neighbour that was binding all along. The other two run the other way: recital 68's limit relieving controllers of any duty to maintain technically compatible systems, and recital 78's duty on producers, an actor no article of the Regulation binds. Three more preamble-only norms lie outside what the instrument can see and were found by hand while adjudicating it -- recital 27's exclusion of deceased persons from the Regulation's scope, which no article contains; recital 71's own 'Such measure should not concern a child', so that the recital this work is named after carries two norms the article drops and the census can see one; and recital 68's 'interoperable', a word in the preamble's format list that Article 20's list omits. The night's own instrument is the sharpest result: the mechanical rule flags exactly one atom in the entire preamble and it is a false positive -- recital 71's 'challenge', which Article 22(3) grants as 'contest' -- while the one genuinely missing atom passes, because 'obtain' occurs elsewhere. On the two cases that matter the machine is wrong in both directions, which is what a string match over a legal text is worth. And the check Session 80 said was missing was run before any claim of novelty and returned something: Humphreys and colleagues mapped recitals to normative provisions at JURIX 2015 and already have the word -- 'norm-like element' -- so this line uses theirs rather than minting another. Position unmoved, thirty-five nights.
